maml:description.maml:para: Tests whether any input element satisfies a condition, or whether there are any elements at all.

The Test-AnyObject cmdlet returns $true if at least one input element satisfies the -Condition script block, and $false if none does. Without a condition, it returns $true if the input has at least one element that isn't $null.

After the first match, the cmdlet stops. It doesn't test the remaining elements, and it stops the commands that send it pipeline input, the same way Select-Object -First does. Those commands produce no more output and don't run their end blocks, although an advanced function's clean block still runs in PowerShell 7.3 and later. Only the pipeline that contains the cmdlet stops, so the statements after it still run. With -InputObject, there's nothing to stop, because PowerShell evaluates the whole argument before the cmdlet starts. To stop a slow source early, pipe it instead.

Each object that comes through the pipeline is one element, even when it's $null or an array, the same as with ForEach-Object. An array or a list that you pass to -InputObject supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one element.
The cmdlet takes its input from the pipeline or from -InputObject, not from both. When it gets both, it writes an error before it reads any input, and outputs nothing.
The cmdlet passes a $null element to -Condition like any other element, so your condition decides what $null means.
By default, an error in -Condition becomes a warning, and the element doesn't satisfy the condition. To have errors reach PowerShell instead, use -ScriptBlockErrorAction.
The test to run on each element. The cmdlet returns $true at the first element for which the script block returns a value that PowerShell treats as $true.

The script block receives each element as $_, $PSItem, and $this, and as its first argument: $args[0], or the first parameter of its param() block. It has to use at least one of these, or the cmdlet fails with a parameter validation error. A variable that appears only in a nested script block doesn't count. Neither does one that appears only in a function that the script block calls, so pass the element to the function as an argument, as in { Test-Big $_ }. You can also pass a function's script block, such as ${function:Test-Big}, whose first parameter receives the element.
Only the first value that the script block outputs counts. PowerShell converts it to [bool] by its usual rules, so 0, '', $null, and no output at all count as $false.
Passing $null is the same as leaving the parameter out, so the cmdlet then tests for elements that aren't $null.
The elements to test. You can pipe them, or pass them to this parameter, but not both.

Each piped object is one element, even when it's $null or an array. An array or a list that you pass to this parameter supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one element.
What happens to errors in -Condition. The default is SilentlyContinue.

With SilentlyContinue or Ignore, each error becomes a warning. The cmdlet runs -Condition with $ErrorActionPreference set to Stop, so the first error that the condition doesn't handle itself, such as an error that a command writes, a failed method call, or a throw, ends the condition for that element. The cmdlet writes the error's message as a warning, and the element doesn't satisfy the condition. An error that the condition handles itself, in a try block or with a command's own -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue or -ErrorAction Ignore, isn't a warning. The warnings follow the cmdlet's -WarningAction, so -WarningAction SilentlyContinue hides them, and -WarningAction Stop makes the first one end the script.

With any other value, -Condition runs with $ErrorActionPreference set to that value, and its errors reach PowerShell unchanged, the same as errors in a ForEach-Object script block. With Stop, an error that the condition writes ends the whole script, as -ErrorAction Stop would, and a failed method call, such as $null.Foo(), ends only the statement that runs the cmdlet. A throw ends the whole script. With Continue, an error that the condition writes appears, and the condition goes on, so the cmdlet uses its output.

With any value, break in the condition leaves the loop that runs the cmdlet. The cmdlet's own -ErrorAction doesn't change any of this, because these errors come from your script block, not from the cmdlet.
You can pipe objects of any type to this cmdlet. Each piped object is one element.
The cmdlet returns $true or $false.

The cmdlet runs one block of each script block that you pass: its process block if it has one, and otherwise its end block, which holds the statements of a script block that has no named blocks. So a script block can't have a begin block, a clean block, or both a process block and an end block, and the block that runs has to contain at least one statement. A script block that breaks these rules fails parameter validation before the cmdlet reads any input.

command:example.maml:title: ------------- Example 6: Handle errors in the condition -------------
command:example.dev:code:

$files | Test-AnyObject { $null -ne (Get-Item $_ -ErrorAction Ignore) } # False, with no warnings

maml:description.maml:para: Creates a List[T] and adds the input elements to it.

The New-List cmdlet creates a System.Collections.Generic.List[T]. T is the type that -GenericType names, or [object] if you don't pass it. A List[object], like an ArrayList, holds elements of any type.
Input elements are converted to T as they're added. An element that can't be converted writes a non-terminating error and isn't added.

The cmdlet skips $null elements unless you pass -IncludeNullElements. A list keeps every element it's given, so $null elements, which usually stand for missing values, would pile up in it. Pass the switch when they matter, for example to keep the list's positions in step with the input.

Each object that comes through the pipeline is one element, even when it's $null or an array, the same as with ForEach-Object. An array or a list that you pass to -InputObject supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one element.
The cmdlet takes its input from the pipeline or from -InputObject, not from both. When it gets both, it writes an error before it reads any input, and outputs nothing.
The cmdlet outputs the list as a single object. When you assign the output to a variable, you get the list itself, even if it's empty or holds only one element.
The element type, T. The default is [object].

You can write the type in any of these forms: a type literal, such as [guid], which PowerShell passes as the string '[guid]'; a type name, with or without brackets, such as guid, '[guid]', or 'System.Guid'; a System.Type object, such as ([guid]); or a script block that contains a type literal, such as { [guid] }. A type literal that contains a comma, as some generic types do, works as it is: PowerShell splits the argument at each comma, and the cmdlet joins the parts back together, as long as they make up a single type.
Press Tab to complete a type name, with or without its brackets and quotes.

The initial capacity, which is how many elements the list can hold before it has to grow. The default is 0. The list grows as it needs to either way, so a capacity only saves the work of growing when you know about how many elements the list will hold.
The elements to add. You can pipe them, or pass them to this parameter, but not both.

Each piped object is one element, even when it's $null or an array. An array or a list that you pass to this parameter supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one element.
Adds $null elements instead of skipping them. In a typed list, a $null element becomes what $list.Add($null) would store, such as 0 in a List[int] or '' in a List[string].

maml:description.maml:para: Creates a HashSet[T], a set of distinct elements, optionally with equality that script blocks define.

The New-HashSet cmdlet creates a System.Collections.Generic.HashSet[T], which holds each distinct element once. T is the type that -GenericType names, or [object] if you don't pass it. Input elements are converted to T as they're added, and the set drops each element that it already holds. An element that can't be converted writes a non-terminating error and isn't added.
Unless you pass -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript, the set compares elements like this:

- [object], the default: two strings are compared the same way as [string] elements, and any other two elements with their own Equals method. Values aren't converted before they're compared, so 1, '1', and [long]1 are three different elements.
- [string]: ordinally, without regard to case. -CaseSensitive makes the comparison case-sensitive.
- Any other type: the type's default equality.
To decide for yourself which elements are equal, pass -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript together. You don't need a compiled IEqualityComparer[T] class, and T can be any type.

An [object] set adds a $null element, which it stores as it is, and only once, so $set.Contains($null) tells you whether the input had one. A set of any other type skips $null elements, because in most types, $null would become a value that wasn't in the input, such as 0 in an [int] set.

Each object that comes through the pipeline is one element, even when it's $null or an array, the same as with ForEach-Object. An array or a list that you pass to -InputObject supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one element.
The cmdlet takes its input from the pipeline or from -InputObject, not from both. When it gets both, it writes an error before it reads any input, and outputs nothing.

Errors in -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript reach PowerShell unchanged, and the cmdlet then outputs no set. See -ScriptBlockErrorAction. The cmdlet's other errors are non-terminating, such as an element that can't be converted to T: the cmdlet writes the error, skips that element, and goes on with the rest.
The cmdlet outputs the set as a single object. When you assign the output to a variable, you get the set itself, even if it's empty or holds only one element.
The element type, T. The default is [object]. With -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript, the script blocks receive elements of this type.

You can write the type in any of these forms: a type literal, such as [guid], which PowerShell passes as the string '[guid]'; a type name, with or without brackets, such as guid, '[guid]', or 'System.Guid'; a System.Type object, such as ([guid]); or a script block that contains a type literal, such as { [guid] }. A type literal that contains a comma, as some generic types do, works as it is: PowerShell splits the argument at each comma, and the cmdlet joins the parts back together, as long as they make up a single type.
Press Tab to complete a type name, with or without its brackets and quotes.
The initial capacity, which is how many elements the set can hold before it has to grow. The default is 0.
The elements to add. You can pipe them, or pass them to this parameter, but not both.

maml:description.maml:para: Creates a SortedSet[T], a set of distinct elements in sorted order, optionally with a sort order that a script block defines.

The New-SortedSet cmdlet creates a System.Collections.Generic.SortedSet[T], which holds each distinct element once and keeps the elements in sorted order. Input elements are converted to T as they're added, and elements that compare as equal are duplicates, so the set keeps only the first of them. An element that can't be converted writes a non-terminating error and isn't added.

Unless you pass -ComparingScript, the set uses the default order of T, which is [string] unless you pass -GenericType. A [string] set compares strings ordinally, without regard to case: it orders them by the codes of their characters, as if they were uppercase. So digits sort before letters, and punctuation such as _ and letters outside ASCII, such as é, sort after Z. The order doesn't depend on your culture or on the PowerShell edition, and a [string] set holds only one of 'a' and 'A'. With -CaseSensitive, a [string] set compares the codes of the characters as they are, so 'a' and 'A' are different elements, and the uppercase letters A to Z sort before the lowercase ones.

T needs a default order: it has to implement IComparable[T], as [int] implements IComparable[int], or be an enum, or be a Nullable[U] whose U qualifies. [string], [int], [datetime], and [version] all qualify. Any other type, such as [object] or [psobject], is an error before the cmdlet reads any input. To sort elements of those types, pass -ComparingScript.
With -ComparingScript, the script block decides the order, and T can be any type. T is then [object] unless you pass -GenericType.

The cmdlet skips $null elements, whatever the element type. In the default [string] set, $null would become '', a value that wasn't in the input, and in an [object] set, the set would put it first without running your -ComparingScript.

Each object that comes through the pipeline is one element, even when it's $null or an array, the same as with ForEach-Object. An array or a list that you pass to -InputObject supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one element.
The cmdlet takes its input from the pipeline or from -InputObject, not from both. When it gets both, it writes an error before it reads any input, and outputs nothing.

Errors in -ComparingScript reach PowerShell unchanged, and the cmdlet then outputs no set. See -ScriptBlockErrorAction. The cmdlet's other errors are non-terminating, such as an element that can't be converted to T: the cmdlet writes the error, skips that element, and goes on with the rest.
The cmdlet outputs the set as a single object. When you assign the output to a variable, you get the set itself, even if it's empty or holds only one element.
The element type, T. The default is [string], or [object] with -ComparingScript. Without -ComparingScript, the type needs a default order, as the description explains.

maml:description.maml:para: Creates a Dictionary[TKey, TValue], optionally with key equality that script blocks define.

[string] keys are compared ordinally, without regard to case unless you pass -CaseSensitive. [object] keys are compared the same way when both are strings, and with their own Equals method otherwise, so 1 and '1' are different keys. Keys of any other type use the type's default equality. To decide for yourself which keys are equal, pass -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript together.
With [object] keys, PowerShell's dot notation, such as $dict.apple, doesn't read or set keys. Use the indexer, $dict['apple'], or pass [string] as the key type.

To start with entries, pipe a hashtable or another dictionary to the cmdlet, or pass it to -InputObject. The cmdlet copies its entries, and converts each key to TKey and each value to TValue. A $null value is copied too, because it may be intentional, and it's converted like any other value, so it becomes '' for [string] and 0 for [int]. An entry whose key or value can't be converted, or that can't be added, such as one whose key is already in the dictionary, writes a non-terminating error and isn't copied.
Errors in -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript reach PowerShell unchanged, and the cmdlet then outputs no dictionary. See -ScriptBlockErrorAction.
The cmdlet outputs the dictionary as a single object. When you assign the output to a variable, you get the dictionary itself, even if it's empty or holds only one entry.
The key type, TKey. The default is [object].

You can write the type in any of these forms: a type literal, such as [guid], which PowerShell passes as the string '[guid]'; a type name, with or without brackets, such as guid, '[guid]', or 'System.Guid'; a System.Type object, such as ([guid]); or a script block that contains a type literal, such as { [guid] }. A type literal that contains a comma, as some generic types do, works as it is: PowerShell splits the argument at each comma, and the cmdlet joins the parts back together, as long as they make up a single type.
Press Tab to complete a type name, with or without its brackets and quotes.

The value type, TValue. The default is [object].

You can write the type in any of these forms: a type literal, such as [guid], which PowerShell passes as the string '[guid]'; a type name, with or without brackets, such as guid, '[guid]', or 'System.Guid'; a System.Type object, such as ([guid]); or a script block that contains a type literal, such as { [guid] }. The initial capacity, which is how many entries the dictionary can hold before it has to grow. The default is 0.

A hashtable or another dictionary whose entries the cmdlet copies into the new dictionary. You can pipe it, or pass it to this parameter, but not both. When you pipe several dictionaries, the cmdlet copies the entries of each one.

Each key is converted to TKey, and each value to TValue. A $null value is converted too, to what $dict.Add($key, $null) would store, such as '' for [string] and 0 for [int]. The $ErrorActionPreference inside -EqualityScript and -HashCodeScript. The default is Stop.

A throw ends the whole script unless this parameter is SilentlyContinue, and break leaves the loop that runs the cmdlet. maml:description.maml:para: Indexes objects in a dictionary by a property or a computed key.

The ConvertTo-Dictionary cmdlet builds a System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary[TKey, TValue] that indexes the input objects by a key: either the value of the property that -KeyPropertyName names, or the value that the -KeySelector script block returns. Each dictionary value is the input object itself, unless you choose a property with -ValuePropertyName or a script block with -ValueSelector.

TKey and TValue are [object] unless you pass -KeyType and -ValueType, whatever the input objects are. Every key and value is converted to these types the way $dict.Add($key, $value) would convert it, including an input object that is its own value. An object whose key or value can't be converted writes a non-terminating error and isn't added. When a value is $null, the dictionary stores what $dict.Add($key, $null) would store: $null for [object], '' for [string], and 0 for [int].

[string] keys are compared ordinally, without regard to case. [object] keys are compared the same way when both are strings, and with their own Equals method otherwise, so 1 and '1' are different keys. To compare keys another way, pass -KeyComparer. With [object] keys, PowerShell's dot notation, such as $byName.Jane, doesn't read or set keys. Use the indexer, $byName['Jane'], or pass [string] as -KeyType.
-DuplicateKeyBehavior decides what happens when two input objects have the same key.

The cmdlet skips input objects that are $null, which have no key or value to select. An object whose key is $null, such as one that doesn't have the property that -KeyPropertyName names, writes a non-terminating error and isn't added, because a dictionary can't hold a $null key, and the error tells you which objects lack a key. A $null value is stored, because it may be intentional, such as a property that's empty on some of the objects. With no input, the cmdlet returns an empty dictionary.

Each object that comes through the pipeline is one input object, even when it's an array, the same as with ForEach-Object. An array or a list that you pass to -InputObject supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one input object.
The cmdlet takes its input from the pipeline or from -InputObject, not from both. When it gets both, it writes an error before it reads any input, and outputs nothing.

-KeySelector and -ValueSelector run under your own $ErrorActionPreference, and their errors reach PowerShell unchanged, the same as errors in a ForEach-Object script block. For example, a throw ends the whole script, and break leaves the loop that runs the cmdlet.
The cmdlet outputs the dictionary as a single object. When you assign the output to a variable, you get the dictionary itself, even if it's empty or holds only one entry.
The objects to index. You can pipe them, or pass them to this parameter, but not both.

Each piped object is one input object, even when it's an array. An array or a list that you pass to this parameter supplies its elements, and $null supplies none. Any other value, such as a string or a hashtable, is one input object. The cmdlet skips input objects that are $null.
The name of the property that holds each object's key. You need either this parameter or -KeySelector. The name can't be empty or white space.
To compute keys with a script block, use -KeySelector. A script block that you pass by position binds to -KeySelector, and one that you pass to this parameter by name is an error.
A script block that returns each object's key. Use it instead of -KeyPropertyName.

The script block receives each object as $_, $PSItem, and $this, and as its first argument: $args[0], or the first parameter of its param() block. It has to use at least one of these, or the cmdlet fails with a parameter validation error. A variable that appears only in a nested script block doesn't count.
The first object that the script block outputs is the key. When it outputs nothing or $null, the cmdlet writes a non-terminating error for the object and doesn't add it.

The name of the property that holds each object's value, or a script block that returns the value, the same as -ValueSelector. $null, an empty string, and white space select nothing, so each object is its own value. Any other value, such as a number or an array of names, is a parameter binding error. You can't use a property name or a script block here together with -ValueSelector.
A script block that returns each object's value. You can't use it with a property name or a script block in -ValuePropertyName.

The script block receives each object as $_, $PSItem, and $this, and as its first argument: $args[0], or the first parameter of its param() block. It has to use at least one of these, or the cmdlet fails with a parameter validation error. A variable that appears only in a nested script block doesn't count.
The first object that the script block outputs is the value. When it outputs nothing or $null, the value is $null, converted to TValue the same way as any other value.
The key type, TKey. The default is [object].

You can write the type in any of these forms: a type literal, such as [guid], which PowerShell passes as the string '[guid]'; a type name, with or without brackets, such as guid, '[guid]', or 'System.Guid'; a System.Type object, such as ([guid]); or a script block that contains a type literal, such as { [guid] }. A type literal that contains a comma, as some generic types do, works as it is: PowerShell splits the argument at each comma, and the cmdlet joins the parts back together, as long as they make up a single type.
Press Tab to complete a type name, with or without its brackets and quotes.
The value type, TValue. The default is [object]. When -DuplicateKeyBehavior is Concatenate, the value type is always [object], and the cmdlet writes a warning if you pass another type.

You can write the type in any of these forms: a type literal, such as [guid], which PowerShell passes as the string '[guid]'; a type name, with or without brackets, such as guid, '[guid]', or 'System.Guid'; a System.Type object, such as ([guid]); or a script block that contains a type literal, such as { [guid] }. A type literal that contains a comma, as some generic types do, works as it is: PowerShell splits the argument at each comma, and the cmdlet joins the parts back together, as long as they make up a single type.
Press Tab to complete a type name, with or without its brackets and quotes.

The IEqualityComparer that compares the keys, such as ([System.StringComparer]::Ordinal) for case-sensitive string keys. It works with any key type. A StringComparer compares two strings as strings, and any other two keys with their own Equals method.
Without -KeyComparer, [string] and [object] keys are compared ordinally, without regard to case when both are strings, and keys of other types with the type's default equality.
What happens when two input objects have the same key. The default is Error. The values are:
- Error: writes a non-terminating error and keeps the first value.
- Skip: writes a warning and keeps the first value.
- Concatenate: keeps every value. A key with more than one value holds a list of them. The value type is then [object], and the cmdlet ignores -ValueType.
You can pipe objects of any type to this cmdlet. Each piped object adds one entry, unless the cmdlet skips it.
